human_tolerance.notes: Highly adaptable: where natural habitat has given way to towns it is found in parks and gardens (German Wikipedia), it is common in the eastern Australian bush and in peri-urban areas (French Wikipedia), and is described as a beneficial urban dweller because it eats garden pests such as slugs and snails (English Wikipedia, species article). It is docile rather than shy of people, but a threat close in is met with a hiss and a run rather than familiarity.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Winter inactivity in the southern hemisphere. The nominate subspecies 'bury themselves in their shelter sites and are not active' in cold weather and 'only leave their shelters on days when the sun is out' (English Wikipedia, Eastern blue-tongued skink). The month window is authored from that southern-hemisphere winter description; no open source gives dated onset and end.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Spring mating. German Wikipedia: the mostly solitary skinks gather to mate between September and November, the southern-hemisphere spring. The English article on the nominate subspecies gives the same three months and notes that they are marked by fights between males.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Male-male combat over females runs through the mating months (English Wikipedia, Eastern blue-tongued skink).

phases.name: young
phases.note: Births. German Wikipedia gives three to four months of gestation after the September-November mating and up to 14 live young per female, so the young phase is placed over the three to four months that follow; the English article on the nominate subspecies reports 6-20 young per year.

vocalizations.description: A loud hiss given with the mouth gaping while the animal flattens its body, stands up sideways to look larger and thrusts out its blue tongue at whatever has frightened it; a bite follows if that does not work. Most often heard when a cat, bird or person comes too close.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives authorship (White, 1790) and status ACCEPTED for usageKey 2462503; ITIS TSN 1182843 gives the same authorship and rank Species under genus Tiliqua (TSN 208919). GBIF's backbone places Squamata at class rank and carries no order for this key, so class Reptilia and order Squamata are taken from the hierarchy in the English article on the nominate subspecies ('the Reptilia class, the Squamata order, the Scincidae family').

external.note: gbif_usage_key and inat_taxon_id are the identifiers given in issue #33 and both resolve: GBIF matches 'Tiliqua scincoides' exactly to usageKey 2462503 (ACCEPTED) and iNaturalist taxon 37456 is the same species. itis_tsn 1182843 from the ITIS scientific-name search; wikidata Q781954 and ncbi_taxon_id 71010 from Wikidata P685 (P685 on Q781954).

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 on Q781954 points to least concern; the English article on the nominate subspecies records the same 'least concern' categorisation from a 2017 consensus.

range.note: Country list from the French article ('toute l'Australie a l'exception de la Tasmanie ainsi que dans les iles Tanimbar et Babar dans les Moluques en Indonésie'), which the German article ('die Heimat ... ist Australien, wo er in weiten Landesteilen aller Bundesstaaten verbreitet ist') and ITIS (geographic division Australia) agree on for Australia, and which the English species article confirms for Tanimbar Island, Maluku, Indonesia. The Indonesian range belongs to the nominate species through its subspecies T. s. chimaerea, which ITIS lists under TSN 1182843. The country-level schema cannot express the Tasmanian exception, so AU is listed and the exception is noted here.

traits.body_plan.note: A lizard, i.e. a vertebrate: 'Tiliqua scincoides is a species of lizard in the subfamily Egerniinae of the family Scincidae (skinks)'.

traits.limb_count.note: Four sprawling legs. German: 'Die Beine sind, im Verhaeltnis zum voluminösen Koerper, geradezu winzig'; the Spanish/French description of five short toes on each fore- and hindlimb confirms four limbs. The model body plan 'quadruped' is the schema's documented plan for lizards as well as mammals.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk only. German: 'Blauzungenskinke sind stets boedenbewohnend' (always terrestrial) and they move 'schleppend-kriechend' (dragging-crawling), though 'koennen aber auch kleinere Hindernisse ueberwinden' (can overcome smaller obstacles) and if flight becomes necessary they can run surprisingly fast. No open source describes a distinct climbing, burrowing or swimming gait, so only Walk is listed; the fast escape run uses the same gait.

traits.thermoregulation.note: 'Blue-tongued skinks are incapable of producing their own body heat, as are all lizards' and they bask to 'maintain their body temperature, which is between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius when they are active'.

traits.skin.note: 'The eastern blue-tongued lizard has smooth skin covered with scales that overlap and have small bone plates' (English); German describes 'sehr glatte, schuppige Haut' with rounded scales and osteoderms.

traits.flight.note: A terrestrial lizard with no wings or gliding membrane; the record declares Walk only, so flight is None.

traits.respiration.note: A reptile breathing with lungs; no source describes any other mode. Judgement from the class assignment in taxonomy, which is the only open-licensed statement of where the species sits.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: the young hatch fully formed. 'Bluetongues are ovoviviparous: the females retain their fertilized eggs and bear their young live' (English, species article) and the young are 'precocial, meaning that its young are more developed and advanced at their time of birth' (English, nominate subspecies). There is no larval stage to record.

traits.nest_type.note: None, because no nest is built: the female gives birth to live young and the precocial young are independent from birth, and the sources describe only cover (logs, rocks, leaf litter, other animals' burrows) rather than a nest. The schema's Ground option would imply a nest site that the sources do not describe.

traits.perching.note: False. The species is described as always ground-dwelling and sheltering among ground objects, leaf litter and dense grass; nothing places it on branches or structures.

traits.senses.note: vision_color: adults and juveniles 'are able to distinguish between color and shape stimuli successfully' (English, nominate subspecies), and the French article describes sensitivity to blue, green and yellow-green but not red. olfaction High: 'they collect microscopic molecules in the air and on surfaces with the tip of their tongue, and then using the tip to deliver the molecules to a sensory organ in the roof of the mouth, which provides their sense of smell' (English, species article) -- the vomeronasal route the tongue-flicking of skinks is built for, so High rather than Med. hearing and the other sense flags are left out because no open source addresses them.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 1.0 kg is not below the schema's 1 kg Small bound, so the class is Medium by the schema's own thresholds (Tiny < 0.05 kg, Small < 1 kg, Medium < 50 kg). See traits.mass_kg for why that mass is used; the size is small for the class only because the schema's bands are wide.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'This lizard weighs approximately 1 kilogram' (English, nominate subspecies); the species article says 'over 1 kg (2.2 lb) in mass'. No open source gives a wild typical mean, so the sourced approximate figure is used as mass_kg and mass_range_kg is omitted rather than invented. The species is long-lived and slow-growing, so a large adult is the best-supported open value; a reviewer wanting a wild mean should treat this as an upper-central estimate, not a mean.

traits.length_m.note: Nose to tail tip, as the schema requires. German: 'wird zwischen 45 und 55 cm lang, wobei der Schwanz etwa 20 cm ausmacht'; French gives '45 a 55 cm de long et jusqu'a 60 pour intermedia'; the English species article gives 'upwards of 60 cm (24 in) in total length (tail included)'. The midpoint of the German range, 0.5 m, is used as the typical total length; the larger figures are the species maxima and the 60 cm in the nominate subspecies is the top of its range.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: No open source gives a standing height. The sourced limb datum is that 'the hind limb length makes up 20% of snout-vent length' with a snout-vent length of 300-320 mm, i.e. hind limbs of 60-64 mm, but a skink sprawls: the belly rests on the ground and the limb runs out sideways rather than holding the body up, so the vertical clearance under the body is only a fraction of the limb length. 0.06 m is therefore the authored height of the body's mid-line, which puts the belly about 2 cm clear of the ground and the back about 10 cm up -- the low-slung read the German article describes ('Die Beine sind, im Verhaeltnis zum voluminösen Koerper, geradezu winzig'). The matching horizontal proportion is leg_length_ratio 0.15; note that the mesh takes its leg length from this field rather than from leg_length_ratio.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The schema asks for a typical wild lifespan and no open source gives one. The English article on the nominate subspecies says 'in captivity, the eastern blue-tongued skink can live in excess of 20 years', the French article '30 ans et plus en captivite', and the species article 'known to live over 30 years' without qualification. The lowest of the sourced figures (20) is used as the most conservative value; with sexual maturity at 561-590 days it is clear this is a long-lived animal.

traits.diet.note: No open source gives quantified shares, so the split is authored judgement anchored on the German article: 'tagaktive Allesfresser, die sich vor allem von Schnecken und groesseren Insekten, aber auch von den Jungtieren einheimischer Nagetiere oder bodenbruechtender Voegel ernaehren' (mainly snails and larger insects, but also young rodents and ground-breeding birds) with 'Ueber die Bedeutung pflanzlicher Nahrung im natuerlichen Lebensraum ist nichts bekannt. Es ist jedoch anzunehmen, dass diese einen wichtigen Teil der Ernaehrung ausmacht' (nothing is known about the importance of plant food in the wild, but it is assumed to make up an important part). Hence invertebrate 0.4 (largest, 'vor allem'), browse 0.25 plus fruit 0.25 for the plant share the sources say is important but unquantified, and vertebrate 0.1 for the vertebrate prey the sources list as occasional. The English species article also lists carrion; no source weights it, so no carrion share is claimed. The capture method is sourced too -- lingual prey capture with a wet adhesion tongue, 'their tongue is coated in a sticky mucus ... for drawing tagged insects back into the mouth'.

traits.social.note: German: 'Die meist solitär lebenden Skinke finden sich ... zur Paarung zusammen' (the mostly solitary skinks come together to mate); English, nominate subspecies: 'in terms of breeding, T. s. scincoides spend most of their time alone'. Solitary, with group_size 1 outside the September-November mating window.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Diurnal. German: 'Blauzungenskinke sind tagaktive Allesfresser' (diurnal omnivores). English, species article: 'Blue-tongued lizards are diurnal: they are active during the day, and sleep at night.' English, nominate subspecies: 'these lizards eat during the day and have been labeled as diurnal.'

traits.defense.note: Flee, and this is a deliberate departure from the issue's suggestion of Freeze. No source describes freezing: the first line of defence is a deimatic display -- 'instead of retreating, bluetongues may hiss, lunge, inflate, and display their blue tongue to startle the animal it considers a threat' -- which the schema cannot express, and the escape is then a run: 'Ist doch einmal die Flucht noetig, koennen die Tiere auch ueberraschend schnell fliehen' (if flight is necessary they can also flee surprisingly fast), with tail autotomy and a bite as last resorts. Of the schema's seven values, Flee is the one the sourced behaviour matches; Hide would describe the cold-weather sheltering, which is modelled instead as the behaviour program's shelter state and as seasonal brumation. The behaviour program also carries a display state that hisses at medium range and only bolts when the threat closes in, so the display is modelled even though traits.defense has to name one value.

traits.wariness.note: judgement: the nominate subspecies is 'said to be docile and shy' and becomes strikingly tame in captivity compared with other lizards, so it tolerates a close observer far better than the small, heavily predated rodents this kit's other small-animal records use (0.7). Not 0 either -- it still bolts into cover when startled and only comes out on warm sunny days.

habitat.use.note: 'Blauzungenskinke sind stets boedenbewohnend' (always ground-dwelling), sheltering in rock clusters, other animals' abandoned burrows, thick leaf litter and dense grass, and avoiding very humid ground. Ground 0.95 is the authored share of time spent foraging and walking on the surface; the 0.05 fossorial share is authored for time spent inside cover -- hollow logs, rock piles, dense leaf litter and other animals' burrows -- which the sources describe as where it shelters but never that it digs.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: leaf_litter. Both languages give leaf litter as the main cover: 'in Bereichen mit dicker Laubschicht oder dichtem Grasbewuchs' (German) and 'take shelter among large objects on the ground like logs or rocks or among leaf litter' (English, nominate subspecies). log_pile and burrow are listed as further shelter resources because the sources also name hollow logs and other animals' burrows.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet, and the diet tags are used directly as the resource tags. The shelter weights are authored from the two sources' cover lists (leaf litter named by both, hollow logs and rock piles by the English nominate article, other animals' burrows by the German article). No water resource is claimed: no open source describes this species drinking.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Adapter with uses_gardens true, from the sources' habitat and behaviour sections: 'they are adaptable animals, often finding habitat in urban and suburban areas, specifically including residential areas of Sydney ... generally considered a beneficial urban dweller because it eats garden pests, such as slugs and snails' (English, species article); 'can be found in suburban and urban areas, specifically in house gardens' (English, nominate subspecies); 'Dort, wo die natuerlichen Lebensraeume Staedten und Gemeinden weichen mussten, findet man sie heute auch in Parkanlagen und Gaerten' (German); 'often found in the bush and in peri-urban areas' (French). Adapter rather than Exploiter because every source describes it as occupying the leftover space in towns, not thriving in dense city. flight_distance_m and road_mortality are omitted: no open source gives them.

seasonal.strategy.note: Brumation, the ectothermic winter dormancy, from the English article on the nominate subspecies: 'In the winter, however, when the weather is cold, lizards bury themselves in their shelter sites and are not active. These lizards only leave their shelters on days when the sun is out, so that they can bask in the sun.' This is inactivity in cold weather rather than true suspended metabolism, which the schema's Brumation is the closest match for; the German article describes no winter dormancy at all, and the sources give no trigger values, so the trigger numbers are authored (see seasonal.triggers).

seasonal.triggers.note: judgement: no open source gives a numeric trigger. Both triggers are authored from the sourced behaviour that the animal is active only in warmth and sun: the enter threshold of 15 C sits well below the sourced active body temperature of 30-35 C (English, nominate subspecies) and is in the range of a mild Australian winter, and 'days: 3' matches the source's 'on days when the sun is out', i.e. sustained cold rather than one cool afternoon. The exit threshold of 20 C is likewise below the active body temperature, so the animal emerges on a mild sunny winter day but not in cold weather, and 'days: 2' allows a warm spell rather than a single sunny hour.

seasonal.phases.note: mating and territorial are sourced: German 'finden sich im Fruehjahr der Suedhalbkugel zwischen September und November zur Paarung zusammen' and English (nominate subspecies) 'September, October and November are mating months ... marked by fights between males in order to attain their first choice female'. young is derived from the sourced three-to-four-month gestation and up to 14 live young (German) and 6-20 young per year (English, nominate subspecies). dormancy is authored to the southern-hemisphere winter from the sourced 'in the winter ... not active' with no dated onset.

seasonal.life_stages.note: duration_days 560 is the lower bound of the sourced sexual maturity age, 'between 561 and 590 days' (English, nominate subspecies), used as the juvenile period. scale 0.35 is the sourced birth size: the young 'koennen rund 1/3 der Kopf-Rumpf-Laenge der Mutter aufweisen' (can be about a third of the mother's head-body length), rounded up slightly for the modelled body. The species is precocial, so no altricial stage is recorded and the young need no parental care.

vocalizations.hiss.note: The hiss is the one sound all four articles describe. German: 'die namensgebende blaue Zunge wird mit weit aufgerissenem Maul praesentiert, waehrend gleichzeitig Zischlaute ausgestoßen werden' (the blue tongue is presented with the mouth wide open while hissing sounds are emitted) and it hisses to intimidate. English, species article: 'when threatened, instead of retreating, bluetongues may hiss, lunge, inflate, and display their blue tongue'. French: 'il a l'habitude de la mettre bien en vue et de siffler bruyamment lorsqu'il est derange' (it hisses loudly when disturbed). Loudness Loud follows 'hisses loudly' / 'hisses loudly'. context Alarm is the schema's value for a sound made at a threat; season_months and time_windows are empty because the sources give no season or time of day; cooldown_s is authored so the display is not repeated every tick. No other call is described in any open source, so none is recorded.

look.note: Colours from the descriptions: 'Die sehr glatte, schuppige Haut ist grau bis braun gefaehrt und mit mehreren Querbaendern versehen' (German, grey to brown with several transverse bands), 'The lizard's back, however, appears dark brown and cream-colored and its head is pale brown. Across its body ... broad black and brown bands. The ventral (abdominal) region of the lizard is a silver or gray color' (English, nominate subspecies) and 'aux ecailles de brun a gris marble de bandes jaunes, orange ou marron, parfois noires. La face interieure est generalement pale' (French). The three dorsal bands in the markings slot are the transverse bands both articles describe; their width, spacing and height on the back are authored judgement. Proportions are authored judgement for a low-slung, heavy-bodied skink from the sourced description and measurements: torso_aspect 2.5 and girth_ratio 1.15 for the 'stout body' / 'voluminösen Koerper', head_scale 0.9 for the large head -- the English article notes that because of the very short legs 'its large head matches the size and shape of a death adder's' -- neck_angle_deg -8 so the head is carried forward in line with the low trunk instead of raised on a neck, tail_ratio 0.8 for a short robust tail (German: about 20 cm of a 45-55 cm animal; English: about 195 mm), beak_ratio 0.3 for a short blunt snout, leg_length_ratio 0.15 for legs that are 'geradezu winzig' relative to the body, and ear_ratio 0.05 because a skink has no external pinna at all, the tympanum being exposed, so the ear boxes are kept almost flat. The blue tongue is the field's namesake feature and is added as an extra_part on the snout in the accent slot; its size and placement are judgement. leg_* is coloured with the pale belly slot because the French article notes the front legs are light and not heavily marked with black. The eye slot is unused because the quadruped mesh has no eye parts.

behavior.note: A species-specific program, fsm-basking-lizard-v1, rather than a shared one. None of the three shared programs models basking: bt-perching-songbird-v1 is a perching bird; fsm-anuran-nocturnal-v1 is explicitly a night amphibian that calls near water in the breeding months, which is wrong for a diurnal live-bearing skink; fsm-ground-forager-v1 runs and could be coaxed into shape, but it has no basking mechanic at all -- its only warm-weather transition goes to a shelter-rest state, and the animal this species actually spends its mornings doing (lying in the sun until it reaches its working body temperature) is the defining part of its day. The program's own states and numbers are authored judgement, with two numbers sourced: the 25-35 C activity window brackets the sourced 'body temperature ... between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius when they are active' and the 'only leave their shelters on days when the sun is out' rule is modelled as a daylight-and-temperature gate out of shelter, and food_tag is the dominant diet share. flee_m 6, display_m 12, calm_m 15 and food_m 12 are authored for a roughly half-metre animal; the two-stage threat response (hiss and show the tongue at range, run only if the threat closes) follows the sourced order 'hisses, lunge, inflate, and display their blue tongue' before the fast escape run, and the display state is the species' vocalised hiss.
